Parliament in flames - if these walls could talk

By: Liz Fish | Paid

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The nation watches in horror as Parliament burns

Unique Selling Point:
A nation in shock and disbelief – with the chamber of the National Assembly going up in smoke. Why did a man set fire to certain offices in parliament and how did he manage to gain access to the precious national keypoint? We track the unfolding drama as media correspondents explore why parliament matters. Parliament embodies the power of voters to shape their country and can be the source of social cohesion – in its existence, South Africa’s Parliament has seen best and worst that humanity can produce. Now, why did a man set fire to the National Assembly chamber and destroy some irreplaceable heritage?


Summary:
We speak to Parliamentary correspondence about the significance of Parliament, the major stories they have covered and the implications of it burning. What's the way forward and how did what appears to be a homeless person gain access and start two fires. Why was nobody monitoring the security cameras- was it only Zandile walking the halls of Parliament from 2am? Security is a major concern with no head of security since 2018 when Zelda Hotlzman was fired and the prolonged outage of power leaving the police with only small monitors to keep an eye. The political opportunism of moving Parliament from Cape Town raises it's head and the mayor offering the City Council Chambers and the newly renovated City hall for SONA 2022. With the statue of Madiba on the balcony it could foot the bill.

Extra Budget Items:
Masa needs to start work very early Wednesday and we will have to shoot the majority of interview on one day so she needs to fly in today. She will fly out on Thursday so needs to nights accomodation

Script:


UPsound 702 Bumper” “we have received reports of a fire in parliament
Script: Ray White acting national managing editor at Eyewitness News was on Talk Radio 702 and one of the first to hear the news
Ray White: So I was doing the weekend breakfast show and it's a Sunday morning, very quiet… 00:00:59:11 I started calling reporters saying you need to get out of bed. We've got a problem here.

UPSOUND “ what I can tell you know is that the fire hasn't been contained it

Script: Parliamentary spokesperson Moloto Mothapo was on holiday when he got the news

Moloto I could not believe it. We had fire last year in March but this was something else

Script: Initially the fire was contained in the old assembly chamber, but there were two fires and when the wind picked up the fire in the National Assembly Building got out of control, threatening to spread to the president's residence. Firefighters said it was one of the hottest fires they’ve fought- it turned into a harrowing 48 hours

Link Never in my life could I have imagined that Parliament would look like this the National assembly gutted broken windows this acrid smell its actually quite devastating being here and actually seeing the effects
Script: A sentiment shared by Mothapo, he’s spent the last 5 years working from an office housed above the National Assembly- now totally gutted

Masa: Moloto your home is on fire…

Moloto : Well, it's my home. It's your home is the home of all South Africans. Uh, it is a very sad moment,we have lost our heritage.

Script: Few know that heritage better, than the correspondents on the parliamentary beat. Gaye Davis, Eyewitness News senior parliamentary correspondent - has spent 27 years walking the maze of corridors in parliament

Gaye: I can't actually get my head around it.

Masa: that was almost like your second home, you were always there.

Gaye: Yeah. Parliament has been the second home to me, and I think that the importance of parliament in a place like Cape Town, which, is often referred to as a European enclave that it was a place where I felt truly South African, where I could be with my fellow compatriots from every walk of life.

Script: Lester Kiewit now a radio host at Cape Talk 567 - spent 7 years of his life covering parliament

Upsound from radio Clip 17 min 051 “a man who is described as homeless

Masa: My first year of reporting at parliament and you invited me to the year end drinks for journalists just down the road here. I mean, there's some beautiful connections that have been formed here.

Lester: Parliament is about the people? You see ministers and you see the president and it's a “hi” as if you were walking into a colleague. It is sometimes sharing a cigarette with an MP in the courtyard.

Script: Journalists that have made the workings of parliament accessible to the public keeping parliamentarians accountable.

Gaye” But I think that what really sticks out for me are the days when we were fighting so hard for the freedoms that really matter.

Script: Like the proposed amendments to the Protection of State Information Bill in 2011 which would have made it easier for Government to keep secrets

Gaye: A pernicious piece of legislation, draconian in its effect and chilling effect on freedom of speech.

LINK Being back here at my old EWN desk brings really brings back memories of my own experience covering parliament, one incident that really stands out for me is the infamous white shirts night when parliamentary security stormed the National Assembly and aggressively kicked out members of parliament
Script: I was called out to assist Davis who was stuck inside. A year earlier, state intelligence tried to silence the press by using technology to block the cellphone signal.

Gaye: Editors and journalists just got up on their feet, holding up their cell phones and actually protested, volubly and protested outside.

Script: After 1994 Parliament's doors were opened and it became the People’s Parliament, and the public was able to sit in on parliamentary committee meetings for the 1st time. Sadly, over the years it’s become less accessible, reflected during the Zuma years with rings of steel and snipers on the roof during SONA, keeping the people out.

Lester: Clip 115 My most powerful moment at parliament was in 2015 when students stormed the gates, I remember them pushing down on these gates I was inside but somehow they came through the Lilly Street entrance …..it was a very tense moment it was an important symbolic moment for South Africa students coming to the seat of the legislature here in Cape Town.

LINKS Parliament is a prism, a microcosm of our country where our history has played out - so it’s unsurprising the range of reactions to the National Assembly burning down. Some have said it’s an attack on our democracy and stability, while others have celebrated it saying it a fresh start.
Script: Renewing the debate to move parliament to Tshwane.
Gaye: But I think more than anything else, we've lost a central place. We have lost our seat of parliament. You are never going to be able to rebuild without taking a great deal of time and money. And what about the staff, You're still going to need parliamentary villages to house MPs who don't live in Gauteng

Script: If the walls of Parliament could speak - they would tell how our history unfolded through the brutal years of repression, to democracy. Reflected in the hundreds of art works housed in The National Assembly, the full extent of the lost is still unkown.

Lester. There is a yellow wood podium inside the National Assembly, where everyone from P.W. Botha to F.W. de Klerk then to Nelson Mandela to Thabo Mbeki to Molante to Jacob Zuma and Cyril Ramaphosa have all stood there. That's a shared collective history that we have lost inside the National Assembly

LINKS Fingers are being pointed in every direction, we have a suspect in court, the National Assembly speaker says she is not responsible. Who switched off the sprinkler systems and why the delay in the fire alarm sounding - questions and more questions
Script: The City of Cape Town initial fire report on Friday answered some of them. The sprinkler system didn’t work - it wasn't serviced since 2017. The fire doors were latched open helping to spread the fire, and it’s unclear if the fire alarm detection worked.
Link This is the back of parliament, in the heart of the City, as you can see the perimeter fence behind me is pretty low, admittedly there are CCTV cameras everywhere but what is the point if they are not being monitored

Script: Somebody was wandering around from 2am, with no eyes on the 300 security camera monitors.

Masa: When you look at what happened here. Can you blame anyone for thinking of elements of the Sabotage?

Lester: We look at the July protests, which had social elements but instigated by political motives. And when something like this happens at the seat of a people's parliament, you have to start wondering and at the moment we have no answers.

Masa: in the interim. Do you not feel that the Speaker of the House should be taking some responsibility for what has happened?

Moloto: how so?

Masa: the buck stops with her?

Moloto: if there is a need for anyone to take accountability for what has transpired here, they will ensure as the leaders and the heads of this institution that happens.

Script: Now all the Correspondents have left are memories and stories- as the forensic experts begin to comb through the ashes. Will they roll out the red carpet here again or will this turn into another neglected museum.
